talk.title: Hyponatremia: SIADH Pathophysiology & the Furst Ratio
talk.subtitle: Why the urine tells you more than the serum — a mechanistic deep dive
guideline_sources: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Hyponatremia (2014, reaffirmed in 2024 context)
European Clinical Practice Guideline on Hyponatremia (ERA-EDTA/ESE/ESI 2014)
Expert Panel Recommendations on Diagnosis and Management of SIADH (Verbalis et al., Am J Med 2013)

sections.heading: Normal Water Homeostasis & ADH Physiology
points: ADH (arginine vasopressin) is synthesized in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, stored in posterior pituitary, and released in response to increased plasma osmolality (threshold ~280 mOsm/kg) or decreased effective arterial blood volume (>7-10% volume depletion)

ADH binds V2 receptors on basolateral membrane of principal cells in the collecting duct, activating Gs-adenylyl cyclase-cAMP-PKA cascade, which phosphorylates aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels and traffics them to the apical membrane
Result: water reabsorption from tubular lumen into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, concentrating the urine (up to 1200 mOsm/kg) and diluting the plasma

Normal suppression: when plasma osmolality falls below ~280 mOsm/kg, ADH is suppressed to undetectable levels, AQP2 channels are internalized, collecting duct becomes water-impermeable, and urine dilutes maximally to ~50 mOsm/kg

Daily obligate solute load is ~600-900 mOsm. Maximum urine dilution = 50 mOsm/kg. Therefore max daily free water excretion = 600/50 = 12 L. This is why it takes enormous water intake (>12-15 L/day) to cause hyponatremia in a normal person — the kidney's diluting capacity is massive when ADH is appropriately suppressed
sections.teaching_pearl: The countercurrent multiplier (loop of Henle) creates the medullary gradient, but ADH is the gatekeeper that determines whether the collecting duct 'uses' that gradient to reabsorb water. Without ADH, water passes right through to the bladder.
sections.board_tip: A urine osmolality less than 100 mOsm/kg in hyponatremia indicates appropriately suppressed ADH — think primary polydipsia or low solute intake (beer potomania, tea-and-toast diet). If urine osm is greater than 100, ADH is active and inappropriately so given the low serum osm.

sections.heading: SIADH Pathophysiology — What Goes Wrong
points: SIADH = continued ADH secretion despite low plasma osmolality and euvolemia. ADH is 'inappropriate' because neither osmotic nor hemodynamic stimuli justify its release
Step 1 — Water retention: persistent AQP2 insertion causes free water reabsorption, expanding total body water by 2-3 L. This dilutes all solutes, producing hypotonic hyponatremia

Step 2 — Volume expansion triggers 'escape from antidiuresis': the mild ECF expansion activates natriuretic peptides (ANP/BNP), suppresses RAAS and aldosterone, and increases renal perfusion pressure. This causes brisk natriuresis (UNa typically >30-40 mEq/L) and maintains clinically euvolemic appearance (no edema, no JVD)

Step 3 — New steady state: the patient reaches a new lower set-point for serum Na. Ongoing water retention is balanced by natriuresis. But the kidney continues to concentrate urine inappropriately, limiting free water excretion
Key lab signature per KDIGO: serum osmolality 100 mOsm/kg (usually >300), urine sodium >30 mEq/L, clinically euvolemic, normal thyroid and adrenal function, no diuretic use

Common etiologies by category: CNS (stroke, SAH, meningitis, TBI), pulmonary (pneumonia, TB, small cell lung cancer), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, oxytocin, opioids, NSAIDs, MDMA), post-surgical pain/nausea (potent ADH stimuli)
sections.teaching_pearl: The natriuresis in SIADH is a COMPENSATION for mild volume expansion — it is NOT the primary problem. This is why UNa >30 is part of the diagnostic criteria and why giving normal saline to SIADH patients can paradoxically worsen hyponatremia (the kidney retains the water and excretes the salt).
sections.board_tip: Hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency both mimic SIADH. Cortisol deficiency causes ADH release via loss of cortisol's tonic inhibition on ADH AND via decreased cardiac output causing hypovolemic ADH stimulation. Always check TSH and morning cortisol (or cosyntropin stim test) before diagnosing SIADH.

sections.heading: The Furst (Electrolyte-Free Water Clearance) Ratio — Predicting Fluid Restriction Response
points: The Furst formula: Ratio = (Urine [Na] + Urine [K]) / Serum [Na]. This estimates the tonicity of the urine relative to serum and predicts whether the kidney is generating or retaining electrolyte-free water
Ratio < 0.5: urine is very dilute relative to serum. The kidney is excreting substantial free water. Fluid restriction will work easily. Restrict to <1.5 L/day
Ratio 0.5–1.0: urine has intermediate tonicity. Fluid restriction may work but must be aggressive (<1 L/day). Clinical response should be monitored closely at 24-48 hours

Ratio > 1.0: urine is MORE concentrated than serum in terms of effective osmoles. Every liter of urine excreted actually returns NET free water to the body. Fluid restriction WILL NOT WORK — you are generating free water with every liter of urine produced. Must escalate therapy

Mechanistic explanation: if urine [Na+K] = 180 mEq/L and serum Na = 130 mEq/L, ratio = 1.38. For every 1L of urine excreted, the kidney removes 180 mEq of monovalent cations but only 130 mEq-worth of tonicity was 'dissolved' in 1L of plasma. The extra water is retained — net free water gain of ~280 mL per liter of urine

Per KDIGO hyponatremia guidance: calculate the Furst ratio at baseline to guide therapy selection. If ratio >1, proceed directly to salt tablets + loop diuretics, urea, or vaptans rather than wasting 48 hours on failed fluid restriction
sections.teaching_pearl: Think of the Furst ratio as answering one question: 'Is the kidney working FOR you or AGAINST you?' If >1, the kidney is making things worse with every drop of urine. Normal saline (Na 154 mEq/L) in SIADH with high urine osmolality can worsen hyponatremia for the same reason — the kidney retains the water and excretes the sodium, generating net free water.
sections.board_tip: Classic board question: patient with SIADH is started on fluid restriction and Na does not improve after 48 hours. Urine Na is 90, urine K is 60, serum Na is 125. Furst ratio = (90+60)/125 = 1.2 — ratio >1 explains the failure. Next step: add oral salt tabs with furosemide (furosemide disrupts the medullary gradient, lowers urine osm, and increases free water excretion) OR oral urea 15-30g/day OR consider tolvaptan.

sections.heading: Treatment Algorithm & Safe Correction
points: SEVERITY TRIAGE: Severe symptoms (seizures, obtundation) = hypertonic saline 3% NaCl bolus 100-150 mL IV over 10-20 min, repeat up to 3 times if needed. Goal: raise Na by 4-6 mEq/L in first 6 hours to relieve brain herniation risk. This is an emergency regardless of the Furst ratio

SAFE CORRECTION LIMIT per KDIGO: no more than 8 mEq/L in any 24-hour period to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS). High-risk for ODS: serum Na 48h, alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease

CHRONIC/MILD-MODERATE SIADH — stepwise per Furst ratio: Step 1: calculate ratio. If 1, skip to Step 2. Step 2: oral NaCl tabs 3-6g/day + furosemide 20-40mg (furosemide inhibits NKCC2 in thick ascending limb, washes out medullary gradient, reduces maximal urine concentration, thereby lowering urine osm and converting the Furst ratio to 30 days, avoid in liver disease (TEMPO 3:3 liver toxicity signal)

DDAVP CLAMP STRATEGY for overcorrection: if Na rises >8 in 24h, give DDAVP 1-2 mcg IV/SQ q8h to stop free water excretion, then infuse D5W to bring Na back down. This 'clamps' the kidney and gives you precise control. Modern proactive strategy: give DDAVP 1-2 mcg at the START of 3% NaCl treatment to prevent unpredictable aquaresis when the SIADH stimulus resolves

ADDRESSING THE UNDERLYING CAUSE is always paramount: discontinue offending drugs (SSRIs are the most common culprit in outpatients), treat infections, resect tumors. SIADH from drugs typically resolves within 2-4 weeks of discontinuation
sections.teaching_pearl: Furosemide in SIADH is counterintuitive — a diuretic for hyponatremia? But the mechanism is elegant: by blocking NKCC2, you destroy the medullary concentration gradient, so even though ADH is still present and AQP2 channels are inserted, there is no osmotic gradient to drive water reabsorption. Urine osmolality drops toward isotonic (~300 mOsm/kg), which lowers the Furst ratio.
sections.board_tip: ODS (osmotic demyelination syndrome, formerly central pontine myelinolysis) presents 2-6 DAYS after overcorrection with dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, locked-in syndrome. MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in central pons (but may be normal in first 48h). Prevention is everything — always calculate your correction rate q4-6h. If you overshoot, DDAVP clamp + D5W immediately.

summary_points: SIADH = inappropriate ADH → AQP2 insertion → water retention → dilutional hyponatremia. The kidney compensates with natriuresis (UNa >30), maintaining clinical euvolemia
Diagnose SIADH: low serum osm, urine osm >100, UNa >30, euvolemic, normal thyroid/adrenal. Rule out hypothyroidism and cortisol deficiency first

Furst ratio = (UNa + UK) / serum Na: if >1, fluid restriction alone will FAIL — the kidney generates net free water with each liter of urine. Escalate to salt tabs + furosemide, oral urea, or tolvaptan
Correct Na no more than 8 mEq/L per 24 hours (KDIGO). Use DDAVP clamp + D5W for overcorrection. High ODS risk: chronic hyponatremia, Na <105, alcoholism, hypokalemia, malnutrition, liver disease
Severe symptoms (seizures, coma) = 3% NaCl 100-150 mL IV bolus immediately, regardless of other considerations

talk.title: HFrEF: The 4-Pillar GDMT
talk.subtitle: Mechanistic Rationale, Clinical Implementation, and Rapid Initiation Strategy per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guidelines
guideline_sources: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure

sections.heading: Pathophysiology: The Neurohormonal Storm That Kills the Failing Heart
points: Core lesion: reduced stroke volume triggers baroreceptor unloading and renal hypoperfusion, activating two lethal neurohormonal axes — the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)

SNS activation: increased norepinephrine causes beta-1-mediated myocyte apoptosis, calcium overload, arrhythmogenesis, and alpha-1-mediated afterload elevation; chronic catecholamine exposure downregulates beta-1 receptors and uncouples signaling — the failing heart becomes catecholamine-toxic

RAAS activation: angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion (sodium retention, potassium wasting, myocardial fibrosis via collagen deposition), and direct cardiac remodeling through AT1 receptor-mediated hypertrophy signaling (MAPK, TGF-beta pathways)

Aldosterone independently promotes endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and perivascular fibrosis — effects NOT fully blocked by ACE inhibitors due to aldosterone escape (non-ACE-dependent aldosterone production rises over weeks)

Natriuretic peptide (NP) system is the body's counterregulatory defense: BNP and ANP cause vasodilation, natriuresis, suppress RAAS and SNS, and have anti-fibrotic and anti-hypertrophic effects — BUT neprilysin degrades them, shortening their half-life and blunting their protective effects

SGLT2 context: the failing heart is energy-starved, relying on inefficient glucose oxidation; ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate) are a more efficient fuel (higher ATP per oxygen consumed); SGLT2 inhibitors shift metabolism toward ketogenesis, improve myocardial energetics, reduce preload via osmotic diuresis/natriuresis, and suppress inflammatory and fibrotic pathways (NLRP3 inflammasome inhibition, reduced interstitial fibrosis)

Net result without treatment: progressive ventricular dilation (eccentric remodeling), worsening mitral regurgitation, falling EF, congestion, arrhythmia, and death — each neurohormonal axis accelerates the others in a vicious cycle
sections.teaching_pearl: HFrEF mortality is driven by neurohormonal toxicity, not just pump failure. This is why inotropes (which increase cAMP and catecholamine signaling) increase mortality, while neurohormonal blockers save lives despite sometimes lowering blood pressure and heart rate.
sections.board_tip: If a question asks why digoxin reduces hospitalizations but NOT mortality in HFrEF (DIG trial), the answer is that it does not block the neurohormonal axis — it is an inotrope/vagotonic, not a disease-modifying agent. All four GDMT pillars modify the neurohormonal storm.

sections.heading: The 4 Pillars: Drug Classes, Mechanisms, and Landmark Evidence
points: PILLAR 1 — ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan) or ACEi/ARB: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, increasing endogenous BNP/ANP levels (vasodilation, natriuresis, anti-fibrotic effects); valsartan blocks AT1 receptors. PARADIGM-HF (2014): sacubitril/valsartan vs enalapril reduced CV death or HF hospitalization by 20% (HR 0.80), with significant reduction in sudden death. Per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA: ARNi is preferred over ACEi/ARB (Class I). Requires 36-hour washout from ACEi before starting ARNi to prevent angioedema (overlapping bradykinin potentiation)

PILLAR 2 — Evidence-based beta-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol ONLY): Block toxic beta-1-mediated effects — reduce myocyte apoptosis, suppress arrhythmia, allow beta-receptor re-sensitization, and lower myocardial oxygen demand. MERIT-HF (metoprolol succinate): 34% mortality reduction. COPERNICUS (carvedilol): 35% mortality reduction even in severe HF (NYHA IV). Carvedilol additionally blocks alpha-1 (afterload reduction) and has antioxidant properties. Start low, titrate slowly — must be euvolemic first. Do NOT use in acutely decompensated wet HF

PILLAR 3 — MRA (spironolactone or eplerenone): Blocks aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor — prevents myocardial and vascular fibrosis, reduces potassium wasting, counters aldosterone escape. RALES (1999): spironolactone in severe HF (NYHA III-IV) reduced mortality 30%. EMPHASIS-HF (2011): eplerenone in mild HF (NYHA II) reduced CV death/HF hospitalization 37%. Eplerenone is selective (no anti-androgen effects — avoids gynecomastia). Monitor potassium and creatinine closely — contraindicated if K >5.0 or eGFR <30

PILLAR 4 — SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin): Benefits independent of diabetes status. Mechanisms: osmotic diuresis/natriuresis (preload reduction), improved myocardial energetics via ketone body utilization, reduced cardiac fibrosis, NLRP3 inflammasome suppression, improved endothelial function. DAPA-HF (2019): dapagliflozin reduced CV death/worsening HF by 26% (HR 0.74) regardless of diabetes. EMPEROR-Reduced (2020): empagliflozin reduced CV death/HF hospitalization by 25%. Benefits additive to other 3 pillars. Fewest hemodynamic barriers — no significant effect on heart rate or BP; well-tolerated even without uptitration

Combined mortality reduction: all 4 pillars together estimated to reduce 2-year mortality by approximately 73% compared to placebo (extrapolated from trials) — no single drug achieves this; the benefit is synergistic because each targets a different node of the neurohormonal cascade
sections.teaching_pearl: Only 3 beta-blockers have HFrEF mortality data: carvedilol, metoprolol SUCCINATE (not tartrate), and bisoprolol. Boards love testing this — metoprolol tartrate is NOT interchangeable. Similarly, not all ACEi/ARBs are validated, but as a class they are accepted; however, ARNi is now preferred.
sections.board_tip: SGLT2i is the easiest pillar to initiate: no titration needed, minimal BP effect, works regardless of diabetes status. Boards may present a newly diagnosed HFrEF patient — per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA, the recommendation is to start all 4 pillars simultaneously or in rapid sequence (not sequentially over months). SGLT2i and low-dose beta-blocker can be started on day 1.

sections.heading: Implementation Strategy: Start Together, Titrate Fast, Add Adjuncts
points: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA paradigm shift: initiate all 4 pillars as quickly as possible, ideally within first 1-4 weeks of diagnosis, rather than sequential add-on over months. Rationale: mortality reduction begins within weeks of initiation; delaying any pillar costs lives

Practical initiation order if hemodynamics constrain simultaneous start: (1) SGLT2i — easiest, no titration; (2) low-dose beta-blocker — if not volume-overloaded; (3) low-dose ARNi (or ACEi if ARNi not available); (4) low-dose MRA. Titrate each to target dose every 1-2 weeks as tolerated

Target doses matter: PARADIGM-HF used sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg BID; MERIT-HF used metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily; EMPHASIS-HF used eplerenone 50 mg daily. Partial dosing provides partial benefit, but target doses are the goal

Blood pressure management: tolerate SBP down to 90 mmHg if asymptomatic. Reduce or eliminate non-GDMT vasodilators (amlodipine, hydralazine) before reducing GDMT doses. Stagger dosing times if symptomatic hypotension

Potassium and renal monitoring: check BMP within 1-2 weeks of starting ARNi and MRA. Mild creatinine rise (up to 30%) is expected and acceptable with RAAS blockade — do not reflexively discontinue. SGLT2i may cause initial eGFR dip (hemodynamic, not structural) that stabilizes

Key adjunctive therapies per 2022 guidelines: IV iron for iron deficiency (ferritin <100 or ferritin 100-300 with TSAT <20%) per AFFIRM-AHF — improves functional capacity and reduces HF hospitalization. Hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate specifically for self-identified Black patients who remain symptomatic on standard GDMT (A-HeFT trial). Loop diuretics for congestion — NOT disease-modifying, used for symptom control only
Device therapy: ICD for primary prevention if EF remains =3 months of optimized GDMT (must re-assess EF — some patients improve). CRT if EF =150 ms, and NYHA II-IV on GDMT
sections.teaching_pearl: Loop diuretics are the most commonly used HF drug but have ZERO mortality benefit. They are for symptom relief only. Never count furosemide as GDMT. A common board trap is a patient on high-dose furosemide and digoxin but not on any of the 4 pillars — the answer is always to add GDMT.
sections.board_tip: For boards: a patient with HFrEF EF 30% on all 4 pillars with persistent symptoms and EF =150 ms — the next best step is CRT-D, not further medication changes. Also, reassess EF at 3 months before ICD implantation — some patients with new-onset HFrEF recover EF with GDMT and no longer need a device.

sections.heading: Special Scenarios and High-Yield Board Pearls
points: ACEi to ARNi switch: mandatory 36-hour washout to avoid angioedema. ARNi inhibits neprilysin (which degrades bradykinin), and ACEi also raises bradykinin — combined effect causes dangerous angioedema. Boards test this washout period repeatedly

Contraindication to ARNi/ACEi/ARB: bilateral renal artery stenosis (entire renal perfusion depends on efferent arteriolar constriction by angiotensin II), history of angioedema, pregnancy. Use hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate as alternative

HFrEF with concurrent atrial fibrillation: beta-blocker primarily for rate control; CASTLE-AF and CABANA support catheter ablation for symptomatic AF in HFrEF (improved outcomes vs medical therapy). Anticoagulate with DOAC per CHA2DS2-VASc (per 2023 ACC/AHA AF guidelines)
HFrEF and diabetes: SGLT2i preferred diabetes agent given dual cardiorenal benefit. Avoid thiazolidinediones (fluid retention worsens HF). Metformin is safe in stable HF
Hyperkalemia limiting MRA or ARNi: use patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate as potassium binders to enable continued GDMT rather than discontinuing life-saving medications
HFrEF in Black patients: A-HeFT demonstrated mortality benefit of hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate added to standard GDMT — this is a 5th agent ON TOP of the 4 pillars, not a substitute
sections.teaching_pearl: The reason ARNi cannot be given with ACEi simultaneously is molecular: both raise bradykinin through different mechanisms (neprilysin inhibition and ACE inhibition), and the combined effect causes catastrophic angioedema. The 36-hour washout allows ACEi-related bradykinin levels to normalize before adding the neprilysin inhibitor.
sections.board_tip: High-yield board question: a patient on enalapril with HFrEF — you want to switch to sacubitril/valsartan. The answer is STOP enalapril, wait 36 hours, THEN start ARNi. If the question offers valsartan as an intermediate step, that is incorrect — no washout is needed from ARB to ARNi (same AT1 receptor mechanism, no bradykinin overlap).

summary_points: HFrEF is a neurohormonal disease: SNS, RAAS, and aldosterone drive remodeling and death; natriuretic peptide degradation removes the body's counterregulatory defense
4 pillars each target a different node: ARNi (RAAS block + NP augmentation), beta-blocker (SNS block), MRA (aldosterone/fibrosis block), SGLT2i (energetics, preload, inflammation)
Per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA: initiate all 4 simultaneously or in rapid sequence — do not delay any pillar; titrate to target doses
Key landmark trials: PARADIGM-HF (ARNi), DAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced (SGLT2i), RALES and EMPHASIS-HF (MRA), MERIT-HF and COPERNICUS (beta-blockers)
Adjuncts: IV iron for iron deficiency (AFFIRM-AHF), hydralazine/ISDN for Black patients (A-HeFT), ICD if EF =150 ms
Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do NOT reduce mortality — never substitute for GDMT

talk.title: COPD Exacerbation & GOLD Guidelines
talk.subtitle: Pathophysiology, Assessment, and Evidence-Based Management

sections.heading: Pathophysiology of COPD Exacerbation
points: Normal airway: β2-adrenergic receptors activate adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA → smooth muscle relaxation. Muscarinic M3 receptors cause bronchoconstriction via IP3/DAG pathway
COPD baseline: Chronic inflammation (IL-8, TNF-α, neutrophil elastase) destroys alveolar walls and increases mucus production. Loss of elastic recoil reduces expiratory flow
Exacerbation trigger: Viral (rhinovirus, influenza) or bacterial (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis) infection increases inflammatory cascade
Cellular mechanism: Increased neutrophil recruitment → elastase release → further airway wall damage. Mucus hypersecretion blocks airways. Bronchial smooth muscle contraction
Gas exchange failure: V/Q mismatch from airway obstruction + loss of alveolar surface area → hypoxemia ± hypercapnia. Increased work of breathing → respiratory muscle fatigue
sections.teaching_pearl: Exacerbations accelerate the decline in FEV1 by causing irreversible structural damage through neutrophil elastase - this is why prevention is critical
sections.board_tip: Hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD exacerbation indicates severe disease with respiratory muscle fatigue, not just airway obstruction

sections.heading: GOLD 2024 Assessment & Classification
points: New ABE groups replace ABCD: Group A (low symptoms, low risk), Group B (high symptoms, low risk), Group E (high exacerbation risk regardless of symptoms)
Exacerbation risk factors: ≥2 moderate or ≥1 severe exacerbation in past year, blood eosinophils ≥300, history of hospitalization
Cardinal symptoms (Anthonisen criteria): 1) Increased dyspnea, 2) Increased sputum volume, 3) Sputum purulence. ≥2 symptoms = likely bacterial
Severity assessment: Mild (outpatient), Moderate (hospitalized), Severe (ICU/respiratory failure/shock)
Blood eosinophils: ≥300 cells/μL or ≥2% predicts ICS responsiveness and guides long-term therapy
sections.teaching_pearl: The shift to ABE classification emphasizes exacerbation prevention as the key outcome, not just symptom control
sections.board_tip: Blood eosinophils ≥300 is the threshold for adding ICS to LAMA/LABA - remember this number for boards

sections.heading: Acute Exacerbation Management
points: Bronchodilators: SABA (albuterol) ± SAMA (ipratropium). Mechanism: β2-agonist increases cAMP, anticholinergic blocks M3 receptors. No evidence for IV theophylline
Systemic steroids: Prednisone 40mg x 5 days per REDUCE trial. Mechanism: Glucocorticoid receptor activation → decreased inflammatory gene transcription (NF-κB inhibition)
Antibiotics: Indicated if ≥2 Anthonisen criteria OR mechanical ventilation. First-line: amoxicillin-clavulanate, azithromycin, or cephalexin targeting H. flu, S. pneumo, M. cat
Respiratory support: NIV first-line for hypercapnic failure (pH 7.25-7.35, PCO2 >45). Mechanism: reduces work of breathing, improves ventilation per Brochard landmark trial
Oxygen: Target SpO2 88-92% to avoid CO2 retention. Higher targets can worsen hypercapnia by reducing hypoxic drive and increasing V/Q mismatch
sections.teaching_pearl: The REDUCE trial showed 5 days of steroids is as effective as longer courses but with fewer side effects - this changed practice
sections.board_tip: NIV contraindications: altered mental status, unable to protect airway, copious secretions, hemodynamic instability, or facial trauma

sections.heading: Long-term Management & Prevention
points: Maintenance therapy: LAMA + LABA first-line. Add ICS if blood eos ≥300 or frequent exacerbations. IMPACT and ETHOS trials showed triple therapy reduces exacerbations
Long-term oxygen: If SpO2 ≤88% on room air at rest. NOTT and MRC trials showed mortality benefit. Mechanism: prevents pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale
Pulmonary rehabilitation: Exercise training + education reduces hospitalizations by improving respiratory muscle strength and self-management skills
Vaccinations: Annual influenza, pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV15+PPSV23), COVID-19. Reduces exacerbation triggers
Smoking cessation: Most important intervention. Nicotine replacement + behavioral counseling doubles quit rates. Slows FEV1 decline from 60-90 mL/year to 30 mL/year
sections.teaching_pearl: Triple therapy (LAMA+LABA+ICS) should be reserved for patients with eosinophils ≥300 or frequent exacerbations due to pneumonia risk with ICS
sections.board_tip: Long-term oxygen requires documented hypoxemia on two occasions 3+ weeks apart while stable on optimal medical therapy

summary_points: COPD exacerbations result from increased inflammation triggering bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion, and gas exchange impairment
GOLD 2024 ABE classification focuses on exacerbation prevention with blood eosinophils ≥300 guiding ICS use
Acute management: bronchodilators + prednisone 40mg x 5d + antibiotics if ≥2 Anthonisen criteria + NIV for hypercapnic failure
Long-term: LAMA+LABA maintenance, add ICS if indicated, pulm rehab, vaccinations, and oxygen if SpO2 ≤88%

talk.title: Complications of Cirrhosis
talk.subtitle: A Mechanistic Approach to Portal Hypertension and Hepatic Failure
guideline_sources: AASLD 2024 Guidance on Ascites and AKI
EASL 2018 Clinical Practice Guidelines on Decompensated Cirrhosis

sections.heading: Pathophysiology: The Portal Hypertension Cascade
points: STRUCTURAL COMPONENT: Hepatic fibrosis and regenerative nodules distort sinusoidal architecture, increasing intrahepatic vascular resistance; activated hepatic stellate cells (myofibroblasts) contract around sinusoids, further raising resistance

FUNCTIONAL COMPONENT: Intrahepatic endothelial dysfunction causes decreased nitric oxide (NO) production and increased endothelin-1/thromboxane A2 within the liver, creating a vasoconstricted intrahepatic bed — this is the OPPOSITE of what happens in the splanchnic circulation

SPLANCHNIC VASODILATION: Portal hypertension triggers upregulation of splanchnic eNOS and excess NO production in the mesenteric vasculature, leading to arteriolar vasodilation, decreased effective arterial blood volume (EABV), and activation of compensatory systems: RAAS, sympathetic nervous system, and non-osmotic ADH release

HYPERDYNAMIC CIRCULATION: To compensate for decreased EABV, cardiac output increases and SVR decreases — this is the 'peripheral arterial vasodilation hypothesis' (Schrier 1988) that unifies ascites, HRS, and dilutional hyponatremia

PORTAL PRESSURE GRADIENT: Normal HVPG is 1-5 mmHg; varices form at HVPG greater than or equal to 10 mmHg (clinically significant portal hypertension); variceal bleeding risk becomes significant at HVPG greater than or equal to 12 mmHg

BACTERIAL TRANSLOCATION: Intestinal mucosal edema from portal hypertension plus gut dysmotility and bacterial overgrowth facilitate translocation of gram-negative organisms into mesenteric lymph nodes and ascitic fluid — the pathogenic basis of SBP
sections.teaching_pearl: The fundamental paradox of cirrhosis: the liver is VASOCONSTRICTED (low intrahepatic NO) while the splanchnic bed is VASODILATED (high splanchnic NO). This single concept explains why TIPS works (bypasses intrahepatic resistance) and why vasoconstrictors work in HRS (constrict the dilated splanchnic bed).
sections.board_tip: HVPG thresholds are high-yield: greater than or equal to 10 mmHg = clinically significant portal HTN and variceal formation; greater than or equal to 12 mmHg = variceal bleeding risk; reduction to less than 12 mmHg or greater than 20% decrease from baseline with NSBB = protective against first bleed.

sections.heading: Major Complications: Presentation, Workup, and Mechanistic Links
points: ASCITES (most common decompensation): Splanchnic vasodilation reduces EABV leading to renal sodium retention via RAAS activation and ADH-mediated free water retention causing dilutional hyponatremia; diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory for new ascites — obtain cell count, albumin (calculate SAAG), total protein, culture in blood culture bottles at bedside

SAAG greater than or equal to 1.1 g/dL confirms portal hypertension (97% accuracy); ascitic fluid total protein less than 1.5 g/dL indicates high SBP risk (low opsonin activity) and qualifies for primary SBP prophylaxis with norfloxacin or TMP-SMX

SBP: PMN count greater than or equal to 250 cells/mm3 in ascitic fluid — treat empirically with ceftriaxone or cefotaxime; DO NOT wait for culture; IV albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 and 1 g/kg day 3 reduces renal failure and mortality (Sort trial 1999 — NNT of 5 to prevent one death)

VARICEAL HEMORRHAGE: Portal pressure greater than or equal to 12 mmHg causes variceal rupture; wall tension increases with variceal radius (Laplace law); management triad per AASLD 2021: (1) IV octreotide (splanchnic vasoconstriction reduces portal inflow), (2) IV ceftriaxone 1g daily x7 days (SBP prophylaxis — 30% of cirrhotics with GI bleed develop SBP), (3) EVL within 12 hours; Primary prophylaxis: nonselective beta-blockers (carvedilol preferred per AASLD) for medium-large varices

HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY: Impaired hepatic urea cycle fails to clear gut-derived ammonia; ammonia crosses BBB, is taken up by astrocytes, converted to glutamine by glutamine synthetase, causing osmotic swelling (Alzheimer type II astrocytosis); treatment per AASLD: lactulose (titrate to 2-3 BMs/day — creates acidic colonic pH trapping NH4+, and osmotic catharsis reduces contact time) plus rifaximin for prevention of recurrence (reduces ammonia-producing gut flora without systemic absorption)

HEPATORENAL SYNDROME-AKI (HRS-AKI): The extreme manifestation of splanchnic vasodilation — profound decrease in EABV causes maximal RAAS/SNS activation and renal vasoconstriction; kidneys are structurally normal but critically underperfused; diagnosis requires: AKI meeting ICA criteria, no response to 48h of diuretic withdrawal + albumin challenge (1 g/kg/day x2 days, max 100g/day), absence of shock/nephrotoxins, no proteinuria/hematuria suggesting intrinsic disease

HCC SCREENING: Cirrhosis of any etiology warrants surveillance with abdominal ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months per AASLD; annual HCC incidence is 1-6% depending on etiology (highest in viral hepatitis); CT/MRI with contrast for characterization using LI-RADS if screening abnormal
sections.teaching_pearl: The Sort trial showed albumin in SBP is specifically beneficial when creatinine is greater than 1 mg/dL or BUN greater than 30 mg/dL or bilirubin greater than 4 mg/dL — these are patients at highest risk for SBP-related renal failure due to worsened effective hypovolemia from the inflammatory cascade.
sections.board_tip: Board favorite: A patient with cirrhosis and GI bleed who is NOT given prophylactic antibiotics has a 30-50% risk of developing a bacterial infection within 7 days. Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily for 7 days is STANDARD OF CARE alongside octreotide and EVL — always pick the answer that includes all three.

sections.heading: Treatment: Guideline-Based Management and Transplant Considerations
points: ASCITES MANAGEMENT (AASLD 2024): First-line is sodium restriction (less than 2g/day) + spironolactone 100mg (start) with furosemide 40mg (100:40 ratio maintains normokalemia); titrate every 3-5 days to max spironolactone 400mg and furosemide 160mg; goal weight loss 0.5 kg/day without edema, 1 kg/day with edema

REFRACTORY ASCITES: Defined as diuretic-resistant (no response to max doses) or diuretic-intractable (complications prevent adequate dosing); options per AASLD 2024: serial large-volume paracentesis with albumin replacement (6-8 g per liter removed when draining greater than 5L) or TIPS (superior to LVP for ascites control, but contraindicated if MELD greater than 18, age greater than 70, HE history, cardiac dysfunction, or portal vein thrombosis)

HRS-AKI TREATMENT (AASLD 2024): First-line is IV albumin (20-40 g/day) + terlipressin (vasopressin V1 agonist that constricts the dilated splanchnic bed, restoring EABV and renal perfusion); CONFIRM trial (2021, NEJM): terlipressin vs placebo — verified HRS reversal in 32% vs 17% (p=0.006); CRITICAL safety signal: respiratory failure in 11% — avoid if baseline SpO2 less than 90% or serum creatinine greater than 5 mg/dL; alternative regimen: midodrine (alpha-1 agonist) + octreotide + albumin when terlipressin unavailable

TRANSPLANT PRIORITIZATION: MELD-Na score (bilirubin, INR, creatinine, sodium) determines organ allocation; sodium added because dilutional hyponatremia reflects severity of splanchnic vasodilation and portal HTN; every decompensating event should prompt transplant referral — 5-year survival of decompensated cirrhosis is only 20-50% vs greater than 70% post-transplant

NSBB CAUTION: Carvedilol/nadolol reduce portal pressure and prevent first variceal bleed and rebleeding; HOWEVER, in refractory ascites with SBP less than 90, mean arterial pressure less than 65, hyponatremia less than 120, AKI, or HRS — STOP nonselective beta-blockers (AASLD 2021) as they may worsen hemodynamics by suppressing the compensatory cardiac output increase (the 'window hypothesis')
sections.teaching_pearl: Terlipressin works mechanistically by directly opposing the fundamental problem: it is a V1 agonist that constricts the pathologically dilated splanchnic vasculature, restoring effective arterial blood volume and renal perfusion. The CONFIRM trial established its efficacy but the respiratory adverse event rate means careful patient selection is essential — avoid in volume-overloaded patients.
sections.board_tip: Board trap: Do NOT give NSBBs to a patient with refractory ascites and SBP less than 90 mmHg — this is the window hypothesis. NSBBs are beneficial in compensated cirrhosis with varices but can become harmful in very advanced decompensated disease by blunting the cardiac output needed to maintain perfusion.

summary_points: Cirrhosis creates a paradox: intrahepatic vasoconstriction (low NO) drives portal hypertension while splanchnic vasodilation (high NO) causes decreased EABV and RAAS/ADH activation — this single mechanism explains ascites, HRS, and hyponatremia
Variceal bleed management per AASLD 2021: ALWAYS give the triad of octreotide + ceftriaxone + EVL within 12 hours
SBP: PMN greater than or equal to 250, treat with cefotaxime/ceftriaxone + IV albumin (Sort trial); secondary prophylaxis with daily norfloxacin or TMP-SMX indefinitely
HRS-AKI per AASLD 2024: terlipressin + albumin is first-line (CONFIRM trial); watch for respiratory failure
HE: lactulose first-line (titrate to 2-3 BMs/day) plus rifaximin to prevent recurrence
HCC screening: ultrasound with or without AFP every 6 months in ALL cirrhotics regardless of etiology
MELD-Na determines transplant priority — refer at first decompensation

visual_memory_card.top_right: HVPG THRESHOLDS: greater than or equal to 10 = varices form; greater than or equal to 12 = bleeding risk
visual_memory_card.bottom_left: VARICEAL BLEED TRIAD: Octreotide + Ceftriaxone + EVL; SBP Rx: Cefotaxime + Albumin (Sort); HRS Rx: Terlipressin + Albumin (CONFIRM)

talk.title: T2DM Management: The Cardiorenal Paradigm
talk.subtitle: Beyond Glycemic Control — Organ-Protective Pharmacotherapy in Type 2 Diabetes
guideline_sources: ADA 2024 Standards of Care in Diabetes

sections.heading: Pathophysiology: Why T2DM Is a Cardiorenal Disease
points: HYPERGLYCEMIA DAMAGES VIA 4 MOLECULAR PATHWAYS: (1) Polyol pathway — excess glucose shunted to sorbitol via aldose reductase, depleting NADPH and generating oxidative stress; (2) Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) — non-enzymatic glycation of proteins crosslinks collagen, activates RAGE receptors on endothelium triggering NF-kB and inflammatory cascades; (3) Protein kinase C (PKC) activation — diacylglycerol accumulates, PKC-beta isoform increases VEGF (retinal leak), TGF-beta (mesangial fibrosis), PAI-1 (prothrombotic state), and endothelin-1 (vasoconstriction); (4) Hexosamine pathway — fructose-6-phosphate diverted to UDP-GlcNAc, modifying transcription factors and increasing TGF-beta and PAI-1

KIDNEY MECHANISM: Hyperglycemia upregulates SGLT2 in proximal tubule, increasing sodium-glucose reabsorption. Less NaCl reaches macula densa, deactivating tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF), causing AFFERENT arteriolar DILATION. Combined with RAAS-mediated EFFERENT arteriolar constriction, this creates GLOMERULAR HYPERFILTRATION (intraglomerular HTN >60 mmHg). Over years this drives podocyte injury, mesangial expansion, GBM thickening, albuminuria, and progressive GFR decline

HEART MECHANISM: Insulin resistance causes myocardial metabolic inflexibility — the heart shifts to near-exclusive fatty acid oxidation, generating more ROS per ATP. AGEs stiffen the myocardial interstitium. Hyperinsulinemia activates cardiac mTOR driving pathological hypertrophy. Endothelial dysfunction from reduced NO bioavailability impairs coronary microvascular function. Result: HFpEF phenotype (diastolic dysfunction) is the most common cardiac manifestation of T2DM, even before overt CAD

CARDIORENAL SYNDROME LINK: CKD increases preload (volume retention), afterload (arterial stiffness, RAAS activation), and uremic cardiomyopathy. HF reduces renal perfusion and activates sympathetic/RAAS systems, worsening CKD. This bidirectional cycle is the cardiorenal axis — and T2DM accelerates BOTH directions simultaneously
sections.teaching_pearl: The key insight of modern diabetology: T2DM is not primarily a glucose disease. It is a cardiorenal-metabolic disease where hyperglycemia is one of several interconnected drivers. The paradigm shift is treating the ORGAN RISK, not just the A1c number.
sections.board_tip: Board question stem: T2DM patient with eGFR 45 and albuminuria — what do you add REGARDLESS of A1c? Answer: SGLT2 inhibitor. The indication is cardiorenal protection, NOT glycemic control. This is the highest-yield concept tested.

sections.heading: SGLT2 Inhibitors: Mechanism of Cardiorenal Protection
points: MECHANISM OF ACTION: SGLT2i block sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 in S1 segment of proximal tubule, preventing reabsorption of ~90g glucose/day (glycosuria) and ~5 mEq sodium per day. This is the LEAST important effect for organ protection. The CRITICAL effect: by increasing NaCl delivery to the macula densa, SGLT2i RESTORE tubuloglomerular feedback, causing AFFERENT arteriolar CONSTRICTION and REDUCING intraglomerular pressure. This is why GFR initially DIPS 3-5 mL/min then STABILIZES — identical to the ACEi hemodynamic dip, but on the opposite arteriole

CARDIAC PROTECTION MECHANISMS: (1) Osmotic diuresis and natriuresis reduce preload without neurohormonal activation (unlike loop diuretics); (2) Shift myocardial fuel from fatty acids toward ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate), which are a more oxygen-efficient fuel — the 'thrifty substrate' hypothesis; (3) Reduce epicardial fat and myocardial inflammation; (4) Inhibit cardiac Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE1), reducing intracellular sodium and calcium, improving mitochondrial function and reducing oxidative stress

LANDMARK TRIALS — RENAL: DAPA-CKD (dapagliflozin): 39% reduction in composite of sustained eGFR decline ≥50%, ESKD, or renal/CV death — benefit seen in patients WITH AND WITHOUT diabetes, trial stopped early. EMPA-KIDNEY (empagliflozin): 28% reduction in kidney disease progression, including patients with eGFR as low as 20. FLOW trial (semaglutide): first GLP-1 RA to show primary renal endpoint benefit — 24% reduction in kidney disease progression in T2DM with CKD

LANDMARK TRIALS — CARDIAC: EMPA-REG OUTCOME (empagliflozin): 38% reduction in CV death in T2DM with established ASCVD — benefit appeared within WEEKS, suggesting hemodynamic rather than atherosclerotic mechanism. CANVAS (canagliflozin): 14% reduction in MACE. EMPEROR-Reduced and DAPA-HF: SGLT2i reduced HF hospitalization and CV death in HFrEF regardless of diabetes status — now standard of care in HF

PRACTICAL PRESCRIBING: Empagliflozin 10mg or dapagliflozin 10mg daily. Can initiate down to eGFR 20 (per ADA 2024 and KDIGO 2024). Continue even if eGFR falls below 20 once started (stop only at dialysis). Hold perioperatively and during acute illness (sick day rules). Counsel on genital mycotic infections (10-15%, more in women), Fournier gangrene (rare but testable), euglycemic DKA (especially with insulin-dependent patients, fasting, or surgery)
sections.teaching_pearl: The initial eGFR dip with SGLT2i is PROTECTIVE, not harmful — it reflects reduced glomerular hyperfiltration. This is analogous to the ACEi dip. Tolerating up to a 30% creatinine rise is acceptable. Stopping the drug because of the dip removes the long-term protection.
sections.board_tip: If a question asks about a T2DM patient on empagliflozin who develops a 20% rise in creatinine after 2 weeks — the answer is CONTINUE the medication. This is the expected hemodynamic effect. Stopping would be the wrong answer.

sections.heading: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: Complementary Cardiometabolic Protection
points: MECHANISM: GLP-1 RAs mimic incretin hormone GLP-1, binding to GLP-1 receptors on pancreatic beta cells (glucose-dependent insulin secretion), alpha cells (suppressed glucagon), hypothalamic appetite centers (satiety and reduced food intake), and vascular endothelium (anti-inflammatory, reduces oxidative stress and foam cell formation). They do NOT cause hypoglycemia as monotherapy because insulin release is glucose-dependent

CARDIOVASCULAR BENEFIT: LEADER trial (liraglutide): 13% reduction in MACE in T2DM with high CV risk. SUSTAIN-6 (semaglutide): 26% reduction in MACE. REWIND (dulaglutide): 12% MACE reduction in broader population including primary prevention. SELECT trial (semaglutide 2.4mg): 20% MACE reduction in overweight/obese patients WITHOUT diabetes — expanding the paradigm beyond glycemia entirely

Per ADA 2024: GLP-1 RAs are preferred over SGLT2i when the PRIMARY indication is established ASCVD or high ASCVD risk, OR when obesity/weight reduction is a priority. SGLT2i preferred when HF or CKD is present. BOTH can be combined when patient has overlapping indications (e.g., T2DM + ASCVD + CKD = metformin + SGLT2i + GLP-1 RA)

KEY SIDE EFFECTS: GI intolerance (nausea, vomiting — dose-titrate slowly), pancreatitis risk (small, monitor), contraindicated in personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 (C-cell tumors in rodent studies — testable). Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 RA with superior A1c and weight reduction (SURPASS trials)
sections.teaching_pearl: Think of SGLT2i as primarily cardiorenal-protective (HF + CKD focused) and GLP-1 RAs as primarily atherosclerotic CV-protective (MACE focused) with powerful weight loss. They work through completely different mechanisms and are additive when combined.
sections.board_tip: Board stem: T2DM with A1c 8.2%, BMI 34, and history of MI — what to add to metformin? Answer: GLP-1 RA (e.g., semaglutide) for ASCVD benefit AND weight loss. If the stem instead says HFrEF or CKD with albuminuria, the answer switches to SGLT2i.

sections.heading: Integrated Treatment Algorithm per ADA 2024
points: STEP 1 — ALL PATIENTS: Lifestyle (Mediterranean or DASH diet, 150 min/week moderate exercise) + Metformin (unless eGFR <30, lactic acidosis risk, or intolerance). Metformin works via AMPK activation in hepatocytes reducing gluconeogenesis, improving peripheral insulin sensitivity, modest CV benefit (UKPDS legacy). Start 500mg BID, titrate to 2000mg. Check B12 levels annually with prolonged use

STEP 2 — CARDIORENAL RISK STRATIFICATION (independent of A1c): Has ASCVD or high ASCVD risk? → Add GLP-1 RA with proven CV benefit (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide). Has HF (HFrEF or HFpEF)? → Add SGLT2i (empagliflozin or dapagliflozin). Has CKD (eGFR 20-60 and/or UACR >200)? → Add SGLT2i. Has overlapping risk? → Use BOTH classes together

STEP 3 — ADDITIONAL GLYCEMIC CONTROL if A1c still above target: Add second-line agents per phenotype — DPP-4i (weight-neutral, modest efficacy, do NOT combine with GLP-1 RA), pioglitazone (insulin sensitizer, fluid retention in HF), sulfonylureas (hypoglycemia risk, weight gain — avoid in elderly), basal insulin (if A1c very high or catabolic features)

STEP 4 — COMPREHENSIVE CARDIORENAL PROTECTION STACK: ACEi or ARB for any albuminuria (UACR >30) — per ADA 2024 and KDIGO. Finerenone (non-steroidal MRA) for T2DM + CKD with persistent albuminuria on max ACEi/ARB — per FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD trials showing reduced kidney and CV endpoints. Monitor potassium when combining ACEi/ARB + SGLT2i + finerenone. High-intensity statin for age 40-75 with T2DM (at minimum moderate intensity per ADA). BP target <130/80

A1c TARGETS per ADA 2024: <7% for most adults. <6.5% if newly diagnosed, long life expectancy, no hypoglycemia risk. <8% for elderly, limited life expectancy, hypoglycemia-prone, extensive comorbidities. ALWAYS individualize — the target is NEVER more important than avoiding hypoglycemia and medication harm
sections.teaching_pearl: The modern T2DM algorithm is ORGAN-FIRST, GLUCOSE-SECOND. You choose SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA based on cardiorenal phenotype BEFORE considering A1c. A patient with A1c 6.8% but eGFR 35 with albuminuria STILL needs an SGLT2i — the indication is kidney protection, not glucose lowering.
sections.board_tip: The finerenone question is increasingly tested: T2DM patient on max-dose ACEi with persistent albuminuria (UACR >300) and eGFR 40 — what to add? Answer: finerenone. Key monitoring: serum potassium (must be <5.0 to initiate). Finerenone is non-steroidal, so less hyperkalemia and gynecomastia than spironolactone. Per FIDELIO-DKD: 18% reduction in kidney composite endpoint.

summary_points: T2DM drives cardiorenal disease through glomerular hyperfiltration (afferent dilation + efferent constriction), AGE-mediated fibrosis, and myocardial metabolic inflexibility — these mechanisms are the targets of modern therapy

SGLT2i restore tubuloglomerular feedback, reduce intraglomerular pressure, provide natriuresis/osmotic diuresis, and shift cardiac metabolism — first-line for T2DM with HF or CKD regardless of A1c (EMPA-REG, DAPA-CKD, EMPEROR-Reduced)

GLP-1 RAs reduce MACE via anti-inflammatory and anti-atherosclerotic effects plus weight loss — first-line for T2DM with ASCVD or obesity (LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, SELECT). Combine with SGLT2i when indications overlap

Per ADA 2024: stratify by cardiorenal phenotype FIRST, then address residual glycemic gap. Full protection stack = metformin + SGLT2i + GLP-1 RA + ACEi/ARB + finerenone (for persistent albuminuria) + statin
Tolerate the initial SGLT2i eGFR dip (up to 30%), initiate down to eGFR 20, individualize A1c targets, and always check potassium when stacking RAAS blockers with finerenone

visual_memory_card.top_right: GLP-1 RA → ASCVD / Obesity (LEADER, SUSTAIN-6, SELECT)

talk.title: Sepsis Bundle: The Hour-1 Approach
talk.subtitle: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 — Physiology-Driven Resuscitation
guideline_sources: Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) 2021 International Guidelines — SCCM/ESICM

sections.heading: Pathophysiology of Sepsis — Why Every Minute Counts
points: TRIGGER: Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs — e.g., LPS, lipoteichoic acid, beta-glucan) bind pattern recognition receptors (TLR4, TLR2, dectin-1) on innate immune cells → NF-kB activation → massive cytokine release (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6)

ENDOTHELIAL INJURY is the central pathologic event: (1) Glycocalyx degradation by heparanase and metalloproteinases → loss of the endothelial permeability barrier → capillary leak → interstitial edema and intravascular volume depletion; (2) Endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) upregulation + inducible NOS (iNOS) induction → excessive NO → profound vasodilation → distributive shock with low SVR

MICROCIRCULATORY DYSFUNCTION: Even with restored macro-hemodynamics, heterogeneous capillary flow persists — some capillary beds are shunted (high flow, no oxygen extraction) while others are stopped (no flow, ischemia). This explains why tissue hypoxia occurs DESPITE a normal or high cardiac output

MITOCHONDRIAL DYSFUNCTION: Reactive oxygen/nitrogen species (peroxynitrite) inhibit complex I and IV of the electron transport chain → cytopathic hypoxia → aerobic glycolysis → LACTATE production even when oxygen delivery is adequate
COAGULOPATHY: Tissue factor expression on monocytes/endothelium → extrinsic pathway activation; simultaneous downregulation of protein C, antithrombin, and TFPI → microthrombi → DIC → organ ischemia

IMMUNE PARALYSIS (late phase): After initial hyperinflammation, compensatory anti-inflammatory response (IL-10, TGF-beta) → monocyte deactivation (low HLA-DR), T-cell apoptosis and exhaustion → secondary infections

NET HEMODYNAMIC PICTURE: Low SVR (vasodilation) + low effective circulating volume (capillary leak) + myocardial depression (septic cardiomyopathy from TNF-alpha, IL-1 depressing contractility) = septic shock
sections.teaching_pearl: Lactate elevation in sepsis is NOT purely from anaerobic metabolism. It also results from catecholamine-driven aerobic glycolysis (beta-2 stimulation of Na/K-ATPase in skeletal muscle) and impaired hepatic lactate clearance. This is why lactate clearance is a better resuscitation target than a single value.
sections.board_tip: Sepsis-3 definition: life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Organ dysfunction = increase in SOFA score of 2 or more. qSOFA (GCS <15, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100) is a bedside SCREENING tool for patients OUTSIDE the ICU — it is NOT part of the formal definition of sepsis.

sections.heading: The Hour-1 Bundle — SSC 2021 Elements
points: ELEMENT 1 — MEASURE LACTATE: Reflects global tissue perfusion and mitochondrial function; if initial lactate >2 mmol/L, remeasure within 2-4 hours to guide resuscitation. Target lactate CLEARANCE of ≥20% per 2 hours (per ANDROMEDA-SHOCK, lactate-guided and capillary refill-guided strategies showed similar 28-day mortality; peripheral perfusion is a valid alternative endpoint)

ELEMENT 2 — OBTAIN BLOOD CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS: At least 2 sets (aerobic + anaerobic from 2 separate sites); each hour delay in appropriate antibiotics increases mortality ~4-7% in septic shock. Cultures before antibiotics maximizes yield to allow targeted de-escalation, but NEVER delay antibiotics if cultures cannot be drawn promptly

ELEMENT 3 — BROAD-SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTICS WITHIN 1 HOUR of recognition: Cover the most likely pathogens based on suspected source; use local antibiogram; consider MRSA/Pseudomonas/fungal coverage based on risk factors. Empiric regimen should have pharmacokinetic optimization (e.g., extended infusion beta-lactams for time-dependent killing)

ELEMENT 4 — RAPID FLUID RESUSCITATION: 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid for patients with hypotension OR lactate ≥4 mmol/L. Start within 1 hour, complete within 3 hours. This addresses the acute intravascular volume deficit from capillary leak and venodilation

ELEMENT 5 — VASOPRESSORS for MAP <65 mmHg: Norepinephrine is first-line (alpha-1 agonism → vasoconstriction to counteract pathologic vasodilation with preserved beta-1 inotropy). Do NOT delay pressors waiting to complete the full 30 mL/kg — early vasopressor use may reduce fluid overload

CRYSTALLOID CHOICE: SSC 2021 suggests balanced crystalloids (lactated Ringer's, Plasmalyte) over normal saline. SMART trial (2018) showed balanced crystalloids reduced the composite of death, new renal replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction (MAKE30 endpoint) vs NS in critically ill patients. BaSICS trial (2021) showed no significant difference overall, but the preponderance of evidence favors balanced solutions, especially in large-volume resuscitation, to avoid hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis which causes renal afferent arteriole vasoconstriction and reduces GFR

SOURCE CONTROL: Identify and intervene on the infectious source as early as feasible (drain abscess, debride necrotic tissue, remove infected device). Delay in source control independently increases mortality
sections.teaching_pearl: The 30 mL/kg is a STARTING point, not a fixed endpoint. After initial bolus, REASSESS with dynamic measures: passive leg raise (increase in pulse pressure or CO >10% predicts fluid responsiveness), pulse pressure variation >13% on mechanical ventilation, or point-of-care echo (IVC variability, VTI at LVOT). STOP fluids when the patient is no longer fluid responsive — fluid overload is independently harmful.
sections.board_tip: Per SSC 2021, norepinephrine is first-line vasopressor. ADD vasopressin (up to 0.03 U/min) as second agent when NE doses are escalating (vasopressin-sparing strategy). Epinephrine is third-line for cardiac output augmentation. Dopamine is NOT recommended except in highly selected patients with bradycardia and low risk of tachyarrhythmia. Phenylephrine is a pure alpha agonist — avoid as first-line since it can reduce cardiac output.

sections.heading: Reassessment, De-escalation, and Adjuncts — SSC 2021
points: REASSESS VOLUME STATUS AND TISSUE PERFUSION within 6 hours: Clinical exam (capillary refill, skin mottling, mental status), serial lactate clearance, urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/hr, dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness (passive leg raise, pulse pressure variation, stroke volume variation)

ANTIBIOTIC DE-ESCALATION by 48-72 hours: Once culture data and sensitivities return, narrow the spectrum. SSC 2021 recommends daily reassessment for de-escalation. Procalcitonin trends can guide antibiotic discontinuation (declining PCT supports stopping antibiotics, particularly in lower respiratory tract infections)

CORTICOSTEROIDS: SSC 2021 suggests IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg q6h or continuous infusion) in patients with septic shock requiring ongoing escalating vasopressors. Mechanism: reverses sepsis-induced relative adrenal insufficiency and restores vascular catecholamine sensitivity by upregulating alpha-1 receptor expression. Based on ADRENAL and APROCCHSS trials — APROCCHSS showed faster shock reversal and improved 90-day mortality; ADRENAL showed faster shock reversal but no mortality benefit
STRESS ULCER PROPHYLAXIS: PPI or H2-blocker in patients with risk factors for GI bleeding (mechanical ventilation >48h, coagulopathy, prior GI bleeding)
DVT PROPHYLAXIS: LMWH preferred over unfractionated heparin; pharmacologic unless contraindicated (active bleeding, severe thrombocytopenia)
GLYCEMIC CONTROL: Target glucose 144-180 mg/dL; avoid tight control (<110) which increased hypoglycemia and mortality in the NICE-SUGAR trial
VENTILATOR MANAGEMENT if ARDS: Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight), plateau pressure <30 cmH2O per ARDSNet protocol; prone positioning for P/F <150
sections.teaching_pearl: ProCESS (2014), ARISE (2014), and ProMISe (2015) collectively demonstrated that protocolized early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) with central venous catheter targeting CVP, ScvO2, and Hct was NOT superior to usual care — as long as the BASICS were done early and well (fluids, antibiotics, vasopressors). This is why SSC 2021 dropped ScvO2 and CVP targets and instead emphasizes dynamic assessments.
sections.board_tip: Classic board question: Patient with septic shock on norepinephrine 0.5 mcg/kg/min, MAP still 58. Next step? Add vasopressin 0.03 U/min (second-line vasopressor per SSC 2021). If still refractory, consider IV hydrocortisone. Do NOT reach for phenylephrine or dopamine first.

sections.heading: Landmark Trials — Evidence Summary
points: ProCESS (2014, NEJM): EGDT vs protocol-based care vs usual care — no mortality difference at 60 days. Established that structured early resuscitation works, but invasive hemodynamic monitoring (CVP, ScvO2) is unnecessary
ARISE (2014, NEJM): Australian/NZ trial confirming ProCESS findings — EGDT did not improve 90-day mortality vs usual care
ProMISe (2015, NEJM): UK trial — same conclusion. Together with ProCESS and ARISE, dismantled the EGDT protocol of Rivers 2001 as the standard

SMART (2018, NEJM): Balanced crystalloids (LR) vs normal saline in 15,802 ICU patients — balanced crystalloids reduced MAKE30 composite (death, dialysis, persistent renal dysfunction). Absolute risk reduction ~1.1%, NNT ~94
BaSICS (2021, NEJM): Balanced vs saline in 11,000+ ICU patients — no significant overall difference in 90-day mortality, but also no harm; reinforces safety of balanced solutions

ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019, JAMA): Capillary refill time-guided resuscitation vs lactate-guided — no significant difference in 28-day mortality, but CRT group received less fluid and had lower 72-hour SOFA scores, suggesting CRT is a reasonable bedside perfusion target
ADRENAL (2018, NEJM): Hydrocortisone vs placebo in septic shock — faster shock reversal but no 90-day mortality benefit
APROCCHSS (2018, NEJM): Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone vs placebo — reduced 90-day mortality in septic shock
sections.teaching_pearl: The shift from EGDT (Rivers 2001) to the current SSC 2021 bundle reflects a philosophical change: from rigid protocol-driven numbers (CVP 8-12, ScvO2 >70%) to dynamic, individualized resuscitation. The principle remains the same — early aggressive recognition and treatment saves lives — but the tools have evolved.
sections.board_tip: If a board question references ScvO2 targeting or CVP-based fluid management in sepsis, recognize this as the OLD Rivers-era EGDT approach. Current SSC 2021 does NOT recommend routine CVP or ScvO2 monitoring. The correct modern approach uses dynamic assessments (passive leg raise, pulse pressure variation, capillary refill, lactate clearance).

summary_points: Hour-1 Bundle: Lactate → Blood cultures → Broad-spectrum antibiotics → 30 mL/kg crystalloid (if hypotension or lactate ≥4) → Vasopressors for MAP <65 (norepinephrine first-line)
Balanced crystalloids preferred over normal saline to avoid hyperchloremic acidosis and renal vasoconstriction (SMART trial)
Norepinephrine first-line → add vasopressin second → consider hydrocortisone for refractory shock
STOP fluids when no longer fluid responsive — use dynamic measures (passive leg raise, PPV, echo) not static CVP
De-escalate antibiotics at 48-72 hours based on culture data and procalcitonin trends
ProCESS/ARISE/ProMISe retired EGDT — early care matters, not invasive monitoring targets

talk.title: DVT/PE Anticoagulation
talk.subtitle: Mechanism-Based Approach to VTE Treatment — From Coagulation Cascade to Clinical Decision-Making
guideline_sources: ASH 2020 Guidelines on Management of Venous Thromboembolism
ESC 2019 Guidelines on Acute Pulmonary Embolism

sections.heading: Coagulation Physiology and Why Anticoagulants Work
points: Virchow's triad revisited at the molecular level: (1) Endothelial injury exposes subendothelial collagen and tissue factor (TF), (2) Stasis reduces local clearance of activated clotting factors by thrombomodulin-protein C pathway and dilution, (3) Hypercoagulability shifts the procoagulant-anticoagulant balance (e.g., Factor V Leiden resists APC cleavage, antithrombin deficiency reduces thrombin neutralization)

Initiation phase: TF-bearing cells bind Factor VIIa → TF-VIIa complex activates Factor X → small amounts of thrombin generated; this thrombin is insufficient alone to form a stable clot but is critical for AMPLIFICATION
Amplification phase: Trace thrombin activates platelets and Factors V, VIII, and XI on the platelet surface, creating a massive burst of tenase (VIIIa-IXa) and prothrombinase (Va-Xa) complexes
Propagation phase: Factor Xa on the platelet surface converts prothrombin to a THROMBIN BURST → fibrinogen cleaved to fibrin → Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin → stable clot

Key therapeutic insight: Factor Xa is the convergence point of intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, and thrombin is the final effector — this is why direct Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) and direct thrombin inhibitors (dabigatran) are so effective; they target the two most critical amplification nodes

Heparin/LMWH mechanism: Binds antithrombin III, inducing a conformational change that accelerates AT-III's neutralization of thrombin (UFH) and Factor Xa (both UFH and LMWH) by ~1000-fold. LMWH preferentially inhibits Xa because its shorter chain length cannot simultaneously bridge AT-III and thrombin

Warfarin mechanism: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) → prevents gamma-carboxylation of Factors II, VII, IX, X and Proteins C and S → these factors cannot bind calcium or phospholipid surfaces → no functional tenase or prothrombinase assembly
sections.teaching_pearl: The reason warfarin is initially prothrombotic: Protein C (half-life ~8 hours) is depleted before Factor II (half-life ~60 hours). This creates a transient hypercoagulable window in the first 24-72 hours — hence the absolute requirement for heparin bridging during warfarin initiation.
sections.board_tip: Board question classic: Patient on warfarin develops skin necrosis on day 3 — think Protein C deficiency (hereditary or functional). The mechanism is exactly the differential half-life depletion described above. Treat with heparin and Protein C concentrate.

sections.heading: Acute VTE Treatment: Drug Selection Algorithm
points: FIRST-LINE for most DVT/PE per ASH 2020: DOACs over warfarin — preferred for superior safety profile (less major bleeding) with noninferior efficacy

Two DOAC strategies — understand the difference: (A) SINGLE-DRUG approach: Apixaban (AMPLIFY trial) or Rivaroxaban (EINSTEIN trials) — NO lead-in heparin required; higher initial dose for 7-21 days provides early anticoagulation intensity. Apixaban: 10 mg BID x 7 days then 5 mg BID. Rivaroxaban: 15 mg BID x 21 days then 20 mg daily. (B) DUAL-DRUG approach: Dabigatran (RE-COVER) or Edoxaban (HOKUSAI-VTE) — REQUIRE at least 5 days of parenteral lead-in heparin before switching
AMPLIFY trial: Apixaban vs warfarin for acute VTE — noninferior for recurrent VTE, SIGNIFICANTLY less major bleeding (0.6% vs 1.8%). This is why apixaban is often first choice
EINSTEIN-DVT/PE: Rivaroxaban vs enoxaparin/warfarin — noninferior efficacy, similar major bleeding, significant reduction in clinically relevant non-major bleeding
RE-COVER: Dabigatran (after heparin lead-in) vs warfarin — noninferior efficacy, less total bleeding
HOKUSAI-VTE: Edoxaban (after heparin lead-in) vs warfarin — noninferior, less clinically relevant bleeding; notably included severe PE patients with RV dysfunction

Warfarin still indicated in: (1) Severe renal impairment with CrCl less than 15-30 mL/min depending on the DOAC, (2) Antiphospholipid syndrome — per TRAPS trial, rivaroxaban was INFERIOR to warfarin with more thrombotic events in triple-positive APS, (3) Mechanical heart valves — per RE-ALIGN trial, dabigatran caused excess thromboembolic events vs warfarin in mechanical valves

Parenteral anticoagulation with UFH preferred over LMWH when: massive PE requiring thrombolysis (short half-life, reversible with protamine), high bleeding risk, severe renal failure (CrCl less than 30), or potential need for urgent procedure
sections.teaching_pearl: Why no heparin lead-in for apixaban and rivaroxaban? Their loading dose strategy achieves therapeutic Xa inhibition within 1-4 hours. Dabigatran and edoxaban were studied only with lead-in, so we replicate trial design. Never extrapolate — always match the protocol.
sections.board_tip: Triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome is a HARD contraindication to DOACs — warfarin with target INR 2-3 is standard. If a board question describes recurrent thrombosis on a DOAC in a patient with lupus anticoagulant, the answer is switch to warfarin. Cite the TRAPS trial.

sections.heading: Special Populations: Cancer-Associated VTE, Massive PE, and Pregnancy
points: Cancer-associated thrombosis (CAT): Historically LMWH was standard (CLOT trial showed dalteparin superior to warfarin). Now DOACs are an option per ASH 2020
HOKUSAI-CANCER: Edoxaban noninferior to dalteparin for recurrent VTE, but HIGHER GI bleeding — particularly with luminal GI cancers (gastric, colorectal, GI-GU mucosal tumors)

CARAVAGGIO trial: Apixaban vs dalteparin in cancer-associated VTE — noninferior for recurrent VTE and NO significant increase in major bleeding including GI bleeding. This made apixaban the preferred DOAC for CAT

Clinical algorithm for CAT: Use apixaban or rivaroxaban UNLESS active GI or GU luminal malignancy (use LMWH), significant drug interactions with cancer therapy (CYP3A4/P-gp), extremes of body weight, or severe thrombocytopenia (platelets less than 50K — dose-reduce or hold)

Massive PE (hemodynamic instability — SBP less than 90 or requiring vasopressors): Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours is first-line per ASH 2020 and ESC 2019. Half-dose alteplase (50 mg) used in some protocols. PEITHO trial showed tenecteplase reduced hemodynamic decompensation in submassive PE but at cost of increased ICH — thrombolytics NOT recommended for submassive PE routinely

Submassive PE (RV strain on imaging/biomarkers but hemodynamically stable): Close monitoring, anticoagulation, escalate to thrombolysis only if clinical deterioration. Catheter-directed therapy (CDT) increasingly used as a middle ground — lower systemic lytic doses

Pregnancy: LMWH is the ONLY appropriate anticoagulant — DOACs cross the placenta (teratogenic), warfarin is teratogenic (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses — especially weeks 6-12). Fondaparinux is a second-line option. Switch to UFH near delivery for epidural safety
sections.teaching_pearl: The PEITHO paradox: Thrombolysis in submassive PE reduced hemodynamic collapse (2.6% vs 5.6%) but increased major hemorrhage (6.3%) and stroke (2.4% vs 0.2%). Net clinical benefit was NOT demonstrated — hence the guideline recommendation against routine use. Reserve for deterioration.
sections.board_tip: Board favorite: Pregnant woman with DVT — answer is ALWAYS LMWH (enoxaparin weight-based, often 1 mg/kg BID). Warfarin is teratogenic. DOACs are contraindicated. Monitor anti-Xa levels (target 0.6-1.0 IU/mL peak, 4 hours post-dose) because pregnancy increases renal clearance and volume of distribution.

sections.heading: Duration of Anticoagulation and Extended Therapy
points: Provoked VTE (major transient risk factor — surgery, immobilization, trauma, OCP/HRT, long travel): 3 months of anticoagulation then STOP, per ASH 2020. Recurrence risk after stopping is low (approximately 3% per year)

Unprovoked VTE (no identifiable risk factor): Minimum 3 months, then REASSESS. ASH 2020 recommends indefinite anticoagulation if bleeding risk is low-to-moderate. Annual recurrence after stopping is approximately 10% in the first year, 5% per year thereafter

Risk stratification for extended therapy: Consider D-dimer after stopping (if elevated, strong predictor of recurrence), sex (men have higher recurrence than women), residual DVT on ultrasound, thrombophilia status, HERDOO2 score for women (Hyperpigmentation, Edema, Redness, D-dimer greater than 250, Obesity, Older age — score 0-1 suggests safe to stop in women)

Extended-phase dosing: After completing initial 6 months, can reduce dose — Apixaban 2.5 mg BID (AMPLIFY-EXT trial) or Rivaroxaban 10 mg daily (EINSTEIN-CHOICE trial) — both showed significantly reduced recurrence vs placebo with minimal excess bleeding. These reduced doses are NOT for the acute treatment phase
Cancer-associated VTE: Continue anticoagulation as long as cancer is active or being treated — no arbitrary stop date. Reassess periodically for bleeding risk
Second unprovoked VTE: Essentially INDEFINITE anticoagulation unless prohibitive bleeding risk — recurrence rate without treatment is extremely high
sections.teaching_pearl: The AMPLIFY-EXT and EINSTEIN-CHOICE trials are practice-changing: After completing initial treatment, reduced-dose apixaban 2.5 mg BID or rivaroxaban 10 mg daily provides approximately 80% reduction in recurrent VTE with bleeding rates similar to aspirin. This is the ideal extended therapy strategy for unprovoked VTE.
sections.board_tip: Duration question framework: (1) Provoked by major transient factor → 3 months and stop. (2) Unprovoked first event → at least 3 months, likely indefinite with reduced-dose DOAC if low bleeding risk. (3) Cancer → continue while cancer active. (4) Recurrent unprovoked → indefinite. Always weigh bleeding risk using HAS-BLED or similar tools.

summary_points: DOACs are first-line over warfarin for most VTE per ASH 2020 — apixaban and rivaroxaban need no heparin lead-in; dabigatran and edoxaban require 5+ days of parenteral lead-in
Warfarin remains standard for antiphospholipid syndrome (TRAPS trial), mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN trial), and severe CKD with CrCl less than 15-30 mL/min
Cancer-associated VTE: Apixaban preferred DOAC (CARAVAGGIO — no excess GI bleeding); avoid DOACs with active GI/GU mucosal tumors (use LMWH)
Massive PE with hemodynamic instability: Systemic thrombolysis first-line; submassive PE: anticoagulation and monitoring, NOT routine thrombolysis (PEITHO)
Provoked VTE → 3 months; Unprovoked → indefinite with low bleeding risk, using reduced-dose DOAC for extended phase (AMPLIFY-EXT, EINSTEIN-CHOICE)
Pregnancy: LMWH exclusively — DOACs and warfarin both contraindicated

talk.title: Gout: Acute and Chronic Management
talk.subtitle: From Crystal Deposition to Treat-to-Target Urate Lowering
guideline_sources: ACR 2020 Guidelines for Management of Gout

sections.heading: Pathophysiology: Why Crystals Form and Why They Cause Inflammation
points: Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism: hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid via xanthine oxidase; humans lack uricase (lost evolutionary mutation), so uric acid cannot be further degraded

Serum urate solubility threshold is approximately 6.8 mg/dL at physiologic temperature and pH; above this, supersaturation occurs and monosodium urate (MSU) crystals precipitate in avascular, cooler, and acidic microenvironments (peripheral joints, tendons, pinnae)

ACUTE FLARE MECHANISM: MSU crystals are phagocytosed by resident macrophages → crystals destabilize lysosomal membranes → activate the NLRP3 inflammasome → caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β to active IL-1β → massive neutrophil recruitment, NETosis, vascular leak, and the classic red-hot-swollen joint

SELF-RESOLUTION: Flares self-limit because anti-inflammatory macrophages release TGF-β, and neutrophil apoptosis with efferocytosis dampens the cascade; crystal coating with lipoproteins also reduces immunogenicity

CHRONIC TOPHACEOUS GOUT: Persistent hyperuricemia → ongoing crystal deposition → granulomatous foreign-body response → tophi formation (organized aggregates of MSU surrounded by macrophages, giant cells, fibrous tissue) → bone erosion and joint destruction

Renal handling: 90% of urate homeostasis is renal; URAT1 transporter on proximal tubule reabsorbs urate, ABCG2 handles intestinal and renal secretion; genetic variants in SLC22A12 (URAT1) and ABCG2 explain much of hyperuricemia risk
Two-thirds of gout patients are uric acid under-excretors, one-third are over-producers; this distinction can guide therapy but all patients benefit from treat-to-target approach
sections.teaching_pearl: The NLRP3 inflammasome is the molecular bridge between crystal deposition and acute inflammation — this is why colchicine (which inhibits NLRP3 assembly and microtubule-dependent inflammasome activation) and IL-1 inhibitors both work in acute gout.
sections.board_tip: Negatively birefringent, needle-shaped crystals under polarized microscopy = MSU = gout. Yellow when parallel to the compensator axis (remember: Yellow = Parallel = Gout, 'YP' like 'Yellow Pages'). Positively birefringent rhomboid crystals = calcium pyrophosphate = pseudogout.

sections.heading: Acute Gout Flare: Diagnosis and Management
points: Classic presentation: explosive monoarthritis of the 1st MTP (podagra) peaking in 12-24 hours with erythema, swelling, and exquisite tenderness; can be polyarticular in advanced disease

Gold standard diagnosis: arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis showing negatively birefringent MSU crystals; WBC count typically 10,000-70,000/μL (inflammatory range); ALWAYS rule out septic arthritis when monoarticular — gout and infection can coexist

Per ACR 2020: First-line acute therapy is any ONE of the following — NSAIDs (indomethacin 50 mg TID or naproxen 500 mg BID), colchicine (1.2 mg then 0.6 mg one hour later, then 0.6 mg BID — low-dose per AGREE trial), or glucocorticoids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day for 5-7 days, or intra-articular if monoarticular)
For SEVERE or polyarticular flares: ACR 2020 conditionally recommends COMBINATION therapy (e.g., colchicine + NSAID, or colchicine + steroid)

IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra off-label, canakinumab) reserved for refractory cases when NSAIDs, colchicine, and steroids are all contraindicated — mechanistically targets the inflammasome product directly
CRITICAL: Do NOT stop urate-lowering therapy (ULT) during an acute flare; stopping ULT shifts urate equilibrium and can paradoxically prolong or worsen the flare
sections.teaching_pearl: Colchicine works by disrupting microtubule polymerization, which inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome assembly, blocks neutrophil chemotaxis, and reduces NET formation. Its narrow therapeutic window means the low-dose regimen (AGREE trial) is as effective as high-dose but with dramatically fewer GI side effects.
sections.board_tip: In CKD patients who cannot take NSAIDs and have contraindications to colchicine (drug interactions with CYP3A4 or P-glycoprotein inhibitors like clarithromycin or cyclosporine), glucocorticoids are the go-to. Colchicine dose MUST be reduced or avoided with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors — colchicine toxicity is potentially fatal (pancytopenia, multiorgan failure).

sections.heading: Chronic Gout: Urate-Lowering Therapy and Treat-to-Target
points: INDICATIONS for ULT per ACR 2020: 2 or more flares per year, any tophus, or radiographic damage from gout; conditionally recommended for patients with CKD stage 3 or greater, uric acid >9, or urolithiasis

ALLOPURINOL is first-line ULT per ACR 2020 — a xanthine oxidase inhibitor; start LOW (100 mg/day, or 50 mg/day if CKD stage 3+) and titrate every 2-4 weeks to target serum urate <6 mg/dL (or <5 mg/dL if tophi present) — this is the TREAT-TO-TARGET strategy

HLA-B*5801 screening is STRONGLY recommended before starting allopurinol in Southeast Asian descent (Thai, Han Chinese, Korean) and African American patients — HLA-B*5801 positivity confers 50-80x increased risk of severe allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS/SJS/TEN), which carries 20-25% mortality

FEBUXOSTAT (selective xanthine oxidase inhibitor) is second-line per ACR 2020 if allopurinol intolerant or fails to reach target; CONFIRMS trial showed febuxostat 80 mg superior to allopurinol 300 mg at achieving target urate, but CARES trial showed a signal for increased cardiovascular and all-cause mortality vs allopurinol in patients with established CV disease — febuxostat carries an FDA black box warning

URICOSURICS: Probenecid (blocks URAT1 reabsorption) is an alternative for under-excretors, but avoid if CrCl <50 or history of nephrolithiasis; lesinurad (URAT1 inhibitor) was used in combination with XOI but has been withdrawn from US market

PEGLOTICASE (pegylated recombinant uricase): reserved for refractory tophaceous gout unresponsive to oral ULT; converts uric acid → allantoin (soluble); risk of infusion reactions and anti-drug antibodies; immunomodulatory co-therapy (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate) improves efficacy by reducing antibody formation (MIRROR and PROTECT trials)

FLARE PROPHYLAXIS: When starting or titrating ULT, concomitant anti-inflammatory prophylaxis with low-dose colchicine (0.6 mg daily or BID) or low-dose NSAID for at least 3-6 months per ACR 2020; ULT CAN be initiated during an acute flare as long as prophylaxis is on board
LIFESTYLE: Limit high-purine foods (organ meats, shellfish), limit alcohol (especially beer — contains guanosine), limit fructose-sweetened beverages; address metabolic syndrome comorbidities
sections.teaching_pearl: The paradox of early ULT flares: when serum urate drops rapidly, partially dissolved crystal surfaces become re-exposed to the immune system, triggering the NLRP3 inflammasome. This is why prophylaxis is essential during ULT initiation — you are mobilizing the crystal burden, not creating new disease.
sections.board_tip: Per ACR 2020, allopurinol should be started at 100 mg (NOT weight-based dosing) and titrated to target. The most commonly tested board concept: you CAN start ULT during an acute flare. The old teaching of waiting 2-4 weeks is outdated. Also: CARES trial — febuxostat had higher CV mortality than allopurinol in patients with pre-existing CV disease, leading to the FDA black box warning. Choose allopurinol first-line, especially in CV patients.

summary_points: Gout results from MSU crystal deposition when serum urate exceeds the solubility threshold of 6.8 mg/dL; crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β → neutrophilic inflammation
Acute flare: NSAID, colchicine (low-dose per AGREE trial), or glucocorticoids; combine agents for severe flares per ACR 2020
Allopurinol is first-line ULT; start low, go slow, treat-to-target (urate <6 mg/dL, <5 if tophi); HLA-B*5801 testing mandatory in Southeast Asian and African American patients before starting
Febuxostat is second-line; CARES trial demonstrated CV mortality signal — carries FDA black box warning in patients with established CV disease
ULT can be started during an acute flare with concomitant anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for 3-6 months per ACR 2020
Pegloticase is reserved for refractory tophaceous gout; immunomodulatory co-therapy reduces anti-drug antibody formation

visual_memory_card.bottom_left: HLA-B*5801: Screen SE Asian + African American BEFORE allopurinol
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: CARES: Febuxostat ↑CV mortality → Black box → 2nd-line only
