talk.title: Acute Ischemic Stroke & tPA
talk.subtitle: Physiology of cerebral ischemia, thrombolysis, and time-critical management
guideline_sources: AHA/ASA 2019 Guidelines for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke

sections.heading: Physiology of Cerebral Ischemia: The Ischemic Core and Penumbra
points: Normal cerebral blood flow (CBF) is approximately 50 mL/100g/min; the brain consumes 20% of cardiac output despite being only 2% of body weight, reflecting extreme metabolic demand and near-zero anaerobic reserve

Ischemic core: CBF falls below 10-12 mL/100g/min — within minutes, ATP-dependent Na+/K+-ATPase fails, causing cytotoxic edema (intracellular Na+ and water influx), irreversible neuronal death, and restricted diffusion on DWI

Ischemic penumbra: CBF 12-22 mL/100g/min — neurons are electrically silent (loss of function) but structurally intact; this tissue survives on collateral flow and is the THERAPEUTIC TARGET of reperfusion

Excitotoxicity cascade: ischemia leads to glutamate release, NMDA receptor activation, massive Ca2+ influx triggering mitochondrial dysfunction, free radical generation, and activation of caspase-mediated apoptosis

The penumbra progressively converts to core over time — this is the biological basis of 'time is brain'; approximately 1.9 million neurons are lost per minute of untreated large vessel occlusion (Saver, Stroke 2006)

Collateral circulation via the Circle of Willis and leptomeningeal anastomoses determines penumbra survival — patients with robust collaterals have larger penumbra-to-core ratios and benefit more from late reperfusion (basis of DAWN/DEFUSE 3 imaging selection)
sections.teaching_pearl: DWI-MRI detects the ischemic core within minutes (restricted diffusion from cytotoxic edema); perfusion-weighted imaging (PWI) or CTP shows the hypoperfused penumbra. The DWI-PWI MISMATCH = salvageable tissue. This mismatch concept is the physiologic foundation for the extended thrombectomy window.
sections.board_tip: On boards, a question showing a patient with a small DWI lesion but a large perfusion defect at 12 hours from last known well is pointing you toward thrombectomy eligibility per DAWN/DEFUSE 3 criteria — answer mechanical thrombectomy, NOT 'too late for intervention.'

sections.heading: tPA Mechanism, Eligibility, and Evidence
points: Alteplase (tPA) is a serine protease that binds fibrin on thrombus surface and converts plasminogen to plasmin, which cleaves fibrin cross-links — this fibrin specificity distinguishes it from older agents like streptokinase, though at therapeutic doses it still causes systemic fibrinolysis
Standard dose: 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg), 10% as IV bolus over 1 minute, remainder infused over 60 minutes — per AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines
NINDS trial (1995): IV tPA within 3 hours showed 30% relative increase in excellent outcomes (mRS 0-1 at 90 days); NNT = 8; established the 3-hour window; 6.4% symptomatic ICH vs 0.6% placebo
ECASS III (2008): extended the window to 4.5 hours with additional exclusions (age >80, NIHSS >25, oral anticoagulant use, history of both DM and prior stroke); NNT = 14; sICH 2.4% vs 0.2%
EXTEND trial (2019): further supported alteplase benefit in the 4.5-9 hour window when perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue (mismatch), reinforcing physiology-guided selection

Tenecteplase: modified tPA with longer half-life (single IV bolus), greater fibrin specificity, and less systemic fibrinolysis; AHA/ASA now recognizes tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as reasonable alternative, especially as a bridging agent before thrombectomy
Key absolute contraindications: active internal bleeding, platelet count 1.7, aPTT elevated, recent intracranial surgery/trauma (3 months), prior ICH, BP unable to be lowered below 185/110 mmHg
sections.teaching_pearl: tPA works best on partially organized fibrin-rich thrombi. Large vessel occlusions (ICA terminus, proximal MCA) have platelet-rich, organized clots that are relatively tPA-resistant — this is why LVO patients need mechanical thrombectomy even after tPA (bridging therapy).
sections.board_tip: Board favorite: patient presents at 3.5 hours with NIHSS 8, age 72 — eligible for tPA under ECASS III extended window. If the stem adds 'age 82 with diabetes and prior stroke' — these are ECASS III relative exclusions. Per AHA/ASA 2019, treatment is still generally recommended in this scenario, but know the original ECASS III exclusion criteria for exam questions.

sections.heading: Thrombectomy, BP Management, and Acute Protocols
points: Mechanical thrombectomy (stent retriever or aspiration): indicated for LVO (ICA, M1, sometimes M2 MCA, basilar) with NIHSS generally ≥6 and small ischemic core
Within 6 hours: SWIFT-PRIME, ESCAPE, MR CLEAN, EXTEND-IA, REVASCAT all showed dramatic benefit — NNT approximately 2.6 for reduced disability

Extended window 6-24 hours: DAWN (clinical-core mismatch using age/NIHSS/core volume) and DEFUSE 3 (perfusion imaging mismatch) showed thrombectomy benefit; this is purely physiology-driven — selecting patients with viable penumbra regardless of clock time

BP management per AHA/ASA 2019: must achieve BP <185/110 BEFORE tPA administration; maintain <180/105 for 24 hours POST-tPA to reduce hemorrhagic transformation risk; use IV labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine
Physiologic rationale for BP control: reperfusion into ischemia-damaged microvasculature with disrupted blood-brain barrier makes hemorrhagic conversion directly proportional to perfusion pressure
In patients NOT receiving tPA or thrombectomy, permissive hypertension up to 220/120 is generally allowed for the first 24-48 hours to maintain penumbral perfusion through collaterals
Post-tPA monitoring: neuro checks every 15 minutes for 2 hours, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly for 16 hours; any decline — stop infusion, emergent CT, check fibrinogen
sections.teaching_pearl: If a patient deteriorates during or after tPA infusion: STOP the infusion immediately, obtain STAT non-contrast CT, send fibrinogen/CBC/PT. If ICH confirmed, give cryoprecipitate (target fibrinogen >200), tranexamic acid, and platelets. Reverse the lytic state first, then neurosurgical consultation.
sections.board_tip: Board trap: patient with LVO at 18 hours from LKW, NIHSS 14, small DWI core — the answer is thrombectomy evaluation with advanced imaging (CTP or MRI), NOT 'window has closed.' DAWN and DEFUSE 3 extended the window to 24 hours for imaging-selected patients.

sections.heading: Secondary Prevention After Acute Ischemic Stroke
points: Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): for minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA (ABCD2 ≥4), start aspirin + clopidogrel within 24 hours, continue for 21 days, then transition to single antiplatelet — per CHANCE and POINT trials
CHANCE (2013): aspirin + clopidogrel vs aspirin alone within 24h of minor stroke/TIA; 32% relative risk reduction in recurrent stroke at 90 days in Chinese population
POINT (2018): confirmed benefit of early DAPT but showed increased bleeding after 21 days — establishing the 21-day DAPT duration sweet spot
Do NOT give antiplatelets within 24 hours of IV tPA — the risk of hemorrhagic transformation is unacceptably high

High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 20 mg): begin immediately; pleiotropic effects include endothelial stabilization, anti-inflammatory action, and plaque stabilization beyond LDL lowering; per SPARCL trial target LDL <70 mg/dL

Atrial fibrillation detected: anticoagulation (DOACs preferred over warfarin per AHA) typically started at 4-14 days depending on stroke size (small stroke earlier, large stroke later to avoid hemorrhagic transformation)
ACE inhibitor/ARB + thiazide for long-term BP control: target <130/80 per AHA/ASA; PROGRESS trial showed 28% reduction in recurrent stroke with perindopril + indapamide
sections.teaching_pearl: The timing of anticoagulation for AF-related stroke follows the '1-3-6-12 day rule' (informal guide): TIA = day 1, small stroke = day 3, moderate stroke = day 6, large stroke with hemorrhagic transformation risk = day 12-14. Always image before starting.
sections.board_tip: Classic board question: minor stroke NIHSS 2, within 12 hours, no tPA given — best next step is aspirin 325 mg loading + clopidogrel 300 mg loading, then DAPT for 21 days per CHANCE/POINT. If tPA was given, wait 24 hours before any antiplatelet.

summary_points: Ischemic penumbra is the therapeutic target — electrically silent but structurally viable tissue that can be rescued with timely reperfusion
IV alteplase within 4.5h (NINDS, ECASS III) and mechanical thrombectomy for LVO up to 24h with imaging selection (DAWN, DEFUSE 3) are standard of care per AHA/ASA 2019
BP must be <185/110 pre-tPA and <180/105 post-tPA to minimize hemorrhagic transformation through disrupted BBB
DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21 days for minor stroke/TIA started within 24h (but NOT within 24h of tPA) per CHANCE/POINT
Secondary prevention triad: antiplatelet or anticoagulation (if AF), high-intensity statin, and BP control <130/80

talk.title: Atrial Fibrillation: Rate vs Rhythm Control
talk.subtitle: Early Rhythm Control in Recently Diagnosed AF

question.stem: A 58-year-old man presents to his cardiologist for follow-up after being diagnosed with atrial fibrillation 6 weeks ago during an emergency department visit for palpitations and dyspnea on exertion. His medical history includes hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a prior ischemic stroke 2 years ago. He was started on apixaban and metoprolol at the initial visit. His current medications include apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and metformin 1000 mg twice daily. His heart rate is 82 bpm and irregular, blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg. An echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 50%, left atrial diameter of 4.2 cm, and mild left ventricular hypertrophy. He reports ongoing fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance despite adequate rate control. His CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Continue current rate control strategy with metoprolol and reassess symptoms in 3 months
Initiate early rhythm control with antiarrhythmic drug therapy or catheter ablation
Add digoxin to the current rate control regimen for better heart rate management
Switch metoprolol to diltiazem for superior rate control
Refer for AV node ablation with permanent pacemaker implantation

question.explanation: This patient has recently diagnosed atrial fibrillation (within the past year), ongoing symptoms despite adequate rate control, and multiple cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, prior stroke, CHA2DS2-VASc of 5). Per the 2023 ACC/AHA Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines, early rhythm control is recommended in patients with AF diagnosed within the past 12 months, particularly in those with cardiovascular comorbidities and persistent symptoms. The EAST-AFNET 4 trial (2020) demonstrated that early rhythm control (initiated within 12 months of AF diagnosis) significantly reduced the composite endpoint of cardiovascular death, stroke, and hospitalization for heart failure or acute coronary syndrome compared to usual care (rate control), with a 21% relative risk reduction (HR 0.79; 96% CI 0.66-0.94). This benefit was observed regardless of whether rhythm control was achieved with antiarrhythmic drugs or catheter ablation. Importantly, the earlier AFFIRM (2002) and RACE (2002) trials, which showed no benefit of rhythm over rate control, enrolled patients with longer-standing AF and did not mandate early intervention. The paradigm shift introduced by EAST-AFNET 4 emphasizes that timing matters — early rhythm control within the first year of diagnosis confers cardiovascular benefit. Anticoagulation with apixaban must be continued regardless of rhythm control strategy given his CHA2DS2-VASc score of 5. The rhythm control approach (either antiarrhythmic medication such as flecainide, dronedarone, sotalol, or amiodarone — or catheter ablation) should be individualized based on patient preference, comorbidities, and structural heart disease.

wrong_explanations.why: Simply continuing rate control and reassessing later misses the opportunity for early rhythm control within the critical 12-month window from AF diagnosis. The EAST-AFNET 4 trial demonstrated that delaying rhythm control beyond 12 months from diagnosis loses the cardiovascular benefit. Additionally, this patient remains symptomatic despite adequate rate control, which further supports pursuing rhythm control rather than a watchful waiting approach.

Adding digoxin would intensify rate control but does not address the patient's ongoing symptoms attributable to AF itself (loss of atrial contribution to cardiac output, irregular ventricular response). Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic window, potential toxicity, and some observational data suggest possible increased mortality. More importantly, it does not offer the cardiovascular outcome benefits demonstrated with early rhythm control in EAST-AFNET 4.

Switching to diltiazem is another rate control strategy and would not address the underlying AF or his ongoing symptoms. While diltiazem is an effective rate control agent, the patient already has adequate rate control (heart rate 82 bpm), indicating that his symptoms are related to AF itself (irregularity, loss of atrial kick) rather than inadequate rate control. Furthermore, this approach misses the window for early rhythm control.

AV node ablation with permanent pacemaker implantation is a last-resort strategy reserved for patients with refractory AF who have failed both pharmacologic rate control and rhythm control strategies, or who are not candidates for catheter ablation of AF. This patient has not yet attempted any rhythm control strategy, making this premature and overly aggressive. AV node ablation also creates pacemaker dependency and does not restore sinus rhythm.

board_pearls: EAST-AFNET 4 showed that early rhythm control (within 12 months of AF diagnosis) reduces cardiovascular death, stroke, and hospitalization for HF/ACS — a paradigm shift from the earlier AFFIRM and RACE trials which showed no benefit but enrolled patients with longer-standing AF.

Anticoagulation decisions should be based on CHA2DS2-VASc score and must be continued regardless of whether rate or rhythm control is chosen; restoration of sinus rhythm does NOT eliminate stroke risk or the need for anticoagulation.

CASTLE-AF demonstrated that catheter ablation of AF in patients with HFrEF (EF ≤35%) reduces all-cause mortality and HF hospitalization compared to medical rate/rhythm control, supporting ablation as first-line in this population.

CABANA showed that catheter ablation reduced a composite of death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, or cardiac arrest compared with drug therapy in the intention-to-treat population (borderline significance), with stronger benefit in the as-treated analysis — supporting ablation as a reasonable first-line strategy.
DOACs are preferred over warfarin for stroke prevention in nonvalvular AF per 2023 ACC/AHA guidelines; warfarin remains indicated for mechanical heart valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis.
teaching_points: The key distinction between EAST-AFNET 4 and AFFIRM/RACE is timing: early rhythm control within 12 months of AF diagnosis confers cardiovascular benefit, whereas late rhythm control in established AF does not show clear superiority over rate control.

Rate control targets: lenient (<110 bpm at rest per RACE II) vs strict (<80 bpm at rest); lenient is acceptable in most patients, but symptomatic patients may benefit from stricter control or rhythm control.

For rhythm control, drug selection depends on structural heart disease: flecainide/propafenone for no structural disease; dronedarone for mild LVH; sotalol for CAD without HF; amiodarone for HFrEF or significant structural disease.
summary_points: Early rhythm control (within 12 months of AF diagnosis) is superior to rate control for reducing cardiovascular events per EAST-AFNET 4; catheter ablation is particularly beneficial in AF with HFrEF per CASTLE-AF; anticoagulation must continue based on CHA2DS2-VASc regardless of rhythm strategy.

visual_memory_card.top_right: 21% reduction in CV death, stroke, HF hospitalization
visual_memory_card.bottom_left: AFFIRM/RACE: No benefit for late rhythm control
visual_memory_card.bottom_right: CASTLE-AF: Ablation reduces mortality in AF + HFrEF
visual_memory_card.center: EARLY = BETTER: Rhythm control wins when started within 1 year of AF diagnosis
